catalog_quote: [Yukawa 1989: 406] While the convention does not use any tone mark, we shall put ´ on a vowel or homorganic nasal pronounced high and nothing on a low one. At the end of a sentence, the word-final short vowel with ´ on it is usually pronounced falling-toned if there is w/y before it or if -V́(R)C or -V́CVC precedes, but otherwise it is pronounced low while the preceding R (if any) is pronounced high or the preceding syllable is pronounced rising-toned if there is no R, R standing for the second half of a long vowel, a vowel standing immediately after another vowel, or a homorganic nasal (N). ... [Johnson 1923-26: 172] Note.—Mention may be conveniently made here of certain words which although they appear to be identical with Kiswahili or other languages differ as regards stress :— Dog is mbúa, not mbwa. Mosquito is mbúu, not mbu. Face is usíu, not uso. Head is mtúe, not mtwe. New (adjective) is -pía (as in the northern dialects of Swahili), not -pya, etc.

new_statements.citation: Johnson, Frederick. 1923-1926. Notes on Kiniramba. Bantu Studies 2: 167-192, 233-268.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote: opened, PDF page 6 = printed p. 172 (running head 'FREDERICK JOHNSON—'); rendered the page scan at 150 dpi and read it: the Note under 'Class 14 (originally identical with 11)' reads exactly as quoted, and the acute accents on mbúa, mbúu, usíu, mtúe, -pía are present in print (the extracted text garbles them, so the image is the check). Surrounding section: the 'Alphabet' section (pp. 168-169, pp. 2-3) lists five vowels and the consonants, notes on r/l, g/k, s/sh, aspiration per Ittameier, and says nothing about stress, tone or length. A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole 62-page extract finds 'stress' only in this Note; the only other prosodic remarks are A. Werner's edi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened states a stress-placement rule. Johnson's only remark on stress is incidental: in five words whose Swahili cognates have a glide (mbwa, mbu, uso, mtwe, -pya), Kiniramba has a vowel sequence with the stress (acute) on the first vowel of the sequence, i.e. on the penult (mbú-a, mbú-u, u-sí-u, mtú-e, -pí-a). That is consistent with penultimate prominence but is not stated as a rule and no other word in the article or vocabulary carries a stress mark. The modern first-hand description, Yukawa 1989 (p. 406, saved), treats Nilamba purely as an H/L tone language ('we shall put ´ on a vowel or homorganic nasal pronounced high and nothing on a low one') with sentence-final falling/rising-tone realisations on the final and penultimate syllables, and never mentions stress; Ngwasi 2021 (§4.2.4) likewise reports lexical tone (nzala 'hunger' vs nzála 'fingers') and a vowel-length contrast, no stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Johnson's forms are citation forms of isolated words; Yukawa's tone description covers verb forms in isolation and at sentence end (phrase-final penultimate rising tone is a phrasal phenomenon, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the same language: Johnson's 'Kiniramba' of the Iramba plateau (Tanganyika), Yukawa's 'Nilamba (kinilamba)' from a Singida-born speaker, Ngwasi's Nilamba (F31) = Glottolog nila1242 / ISO nim. Masele 2001 distinguishes a 'Kinilamba central' dialect but none of the stress/tone remarks are dialect-specific.

tone_statements.summary: Two-level (H vs L/unmarked) Bantu tone system with the mora (incl. second half of long vowels and moraic nasal) as tone-bearing unit; lexical H/L verb classes; tonally contrasting prefix sets; positional (sentence-final) H realisation/shift rules.

sources.note: 'Alphabet' section (pp. 168-169) gives only segments; no stress or tone rule. Sole stress remark is an incidental Note on p. 172 listing words that 'differ as regards stress' from Swahili, with acute accents on the penultimate vowel of final vowel sequences (mbúa, mbúu, usíu, mtúe, -pía). Editorial footnotes (A. Werner) ask whether homophones are 'distinguished by tone'; vocabulary marks no stress or tone.

sources.note: A dedicated chapter (c. 24 pp.) analysing the tone ('accent' in Yukawa's terminology = H vs. unmarked L) patterns of Nilamba verb forms - infinitive, tense/aspect forms, with and without object prefixes - within a 36-language comparative study of Bantu verb tonology; expected to restate and systematise the H/L analysis of Yukawa 1989 (two tonal verb classes, prefix-conditioned patterns, sentence-final falling/rising realisations) and to place Nilamba in his cross-Bantu typology of verb-tone systems. Chapter text not opened (in-library access only).
